channel.title: AstroAlert – what's happening in space
channel.description: A daily updated guide to astronomical and space events: eclipses, conjunctions, meteor showers, rocket launches, aurorae and close approaches of asteroids.

item.title: Falcon 9 Block 5 | OneWeb 21
item.description:
30.11.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of Falcon 9 Block 5, operated by SpaceX. Site: Vandenberg SFB, CA, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: A batch of 32 satellites for the OneWeb satellite constellation, which is intended to provide global Internet broadband service for individual consumers. The constellation is planned to have around 648 microsatellites (of which 60 are spares), around 150 kg each, operating in Ku-band from low Earth orbit. item.title: Asteroid 2017 WJ2 passes by
item.description:
05.11.2026, 04:22 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 88–197 m will pass Earth at 5.98 million km, or 15.6 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 11.8 km/s. For scale: roughly the size of a large apartment block. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. The pass is entirely safe – approaches like this happen regularly and are tracked as a matter of routine.

item.title: Uranus at opposition
item.description:
30.11.2027, 09:39 UTC

Uranus lies opposite the Sun – it rises at sunset, culminates around midnight and shines at its brightest of the season. Distance from Earth: 18.36 au (2,747 million km; its light takes 153 minutes to reach us). The planet is in Taurus. At the edge of naked-eye visibility, easy in binoculars.

item.title: The Moon meets Venus
item.description:
30.11.2027, 13:38 UTC

item.title: Leonids meteor shower peak
item.description:
17.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

A shower that roughly every 33 years erupts into a storm with thousands of meteors an hour. In ordinary years it is quiet. At maximum, up to 15 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Leo. Unfortunately the Moon will be 89% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Greatest western elongation of Mercury (19°)
item.description:
04.11.2027, 08:45 UTC

Mercury stands 19° from the Sun – the best chance this season to catch the planet in the morning, just before sunrise. The hardest planet to catch – it never strays far from the Sun. Look for it low above the eastern horizon during twilight.

item.title: Southern Taurids meteor shower peak
item.description:
05.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

Few meteors, but an unusual share of fireballs – slow, very bright and worth the wait. At maximum, up to 5 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Taurus. A Moon 38% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
